text: Whether a team runs Scrum sprints or something looser, almost every IT team tracks its actual work on a Kanban-style board — this lesson is about reading one correctly.

Each column represents one status work passes through — Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review, Done. Each card represents one discrete piece of work, with an owner, a description, and usually a priority. As work advances, the card physically moves one column to the right — a live picture of where everything stands.

A column tells you where a card is; a status label tells you how it's actually doing. Off Track means the work is simply taking longer than planned — normal, usually just needs more time. Blocked means the work has hit a hard stop entirely outside the owner's control, and no amount of their own effort moves it forward until that's resolved.

A WIP limit caps how many cards can sit in one column at once. That sounds backwards — wouldn't starting more in parallel get more done? In practice, a developer juggling five things at once is really context-switching between five half-finished tasks, slower overall than finishing one before starting the next. A WIP limit forces the team to actually finish work, not just start it.

Kanban boards aren't one specific product — they're a pattern across several real tools. Jira is the most common in software and data teams; Azure DevOps Boards is tightly wired into Azure repos and pipelines; Trello suits smaller teams; GitHub Projects links boards directly to issues and pull requests. The columns, cards, and WIP limits work the same regardless of which logo is on screen.
